text: When renaming or replacing a shared Wagtail block, update all associated artifacts and usages: rename its template file to the snake_case equivalent of the new class name and update template references; update all imports and usages so the generic built-in block is used where no extra behavior is needed and the custom block is used only where its added behavior is required.
reason: Keeps templates, imports, and block usage consistent and intentional after a block rename or replacement.
common_pattern: Refactoring a Wagtail block requires updating coupled artifacts and usages consistently with the new block name and intended behavior.

text: When modifying demo fixture users in `bakerydemo/base/fixtures/bakerydemo.json`, document each fixture user's existence and intended purpose, use realistic human-like identities for new users rather than generic role-based placeholders, and ensure every active user that needs a `wagtailusers.userprofile` has one (omit profiles only for intentionally excluded users such as inactive users).
reason: Fixture users encode non-obvious testing and benchmarking assumptions, and missing or undocumented fixture profiles can break demo behavior or leave future maintainers unaware of why accounts exist.
common_pattern: Conventions for demo fixture user accounts: document their existence and purpose, prefer realistic identities for new fixture users, and keep profile records complete for active users.

text: Keep at least one usage of any specialized wrapper block (and of the underlying chooser block it exercises) somewhere in the demo block set so base Wagtail chooser blocks (e.g. `ImageChooserBlock`) retain test/demo coverage; place reusable content blocks in `BaseStreamBlock` so they can be composed at arbitrary points rather than as one-off standalone `StreamBlock`s.
reason: Preserves demo/test coverage for underlying chooser blocks and keeps content composable across existing content areas.
common_pattern: Wagtail StreamField/block composition conventions in bakerydemo: prefer using Wagtail's built-in blocks directly and keep custom wrapper blocks minimal, purpose-named, and only for genuinely added behavior.

text: Methods that retrieve or compute related data should be named `get_<noun>` where `<noun>` precisely names the returned entity (e.g., `get_posts()` rather than `blogs()` when returning individual posts), and should be implemented as regular methods rather than `@property`.
reason: Fosters consistency with project conventions (`get_` prefix for retrieval) and makes clear that the method performs work or a query, avoiding ambiguity between a container and its individual entries.
common_pattern: Data-retrieval/computation methods should use a `get_` prefix with a precise noun naming the returned entity, and be implemented as regular methods (not `@property`).

text: Use sentence-case `verbose_name`/`verbose_name_plural` in Django/Wagtail model metadata and let Django/Wagtail apply `capfirst()` when display capitalization is needed; set explicit labels for acronym/initialism fields (e.g. `url` -> "URL"). Make user-facing field labels (`verbose_name`, `help_text`, admin/form/block labels) self-explanatory: spell out or define domain-specific acronyms, rename or override `verbose_name` when a field name is ambiguous for its model context (rather than adding a new model), omit redundant labels that only restate the field identifier, use `Meta.label_format` with `{field_name}` placeholders and concise labels for multi-field `StructBlock` subclasses, and give `ChoiceBlock` choices human-readable, consistently capitalized display labels distinct from their lowercase stored values. Refer to Django fields/classes by their real names (`ForeignKey`) or plain English ("foreign key"), never malformed camelCase such as `foreignKey`.
reason: Keeps label wording and code references accurate and presentation-agnostic across Django model metadata and Wagtail form/block fields.
scope: global: Django model metadata and Wagtail form/block field labels
common_pattern: Conventions for Django/Wagtail user-facing field labels (`verbose_name`, `help_text`, admin labels): how they should be capitalized and how they should be phrased for clarity. Two distinct sub-patterns emerge — (a) capitalization/casing correctness, and (b) clarity/legibility of the label text.

text: Name CSS custom properties by the broad semantic role of the value that covers all its actual use cases, not by ordinal hierarchy (`primary`/`secondary`) when that is misleading, and not by a single element (`--font--headings`) when the value is reused elsewhere.
reason: Names that imply an ordinal rank or a single element become misleading when the value is used in the opposite context or reused across many contexts; role-based names communicate intent and keep styles maintainable.
common_pattern: CSS custom properties (design tokens) should be used consistently in stylesheets: variables must be referenced instead of hardcoded values for colors and fonts, and variables must be named by broad semantic role that reflects actual usage rather than by ordinal rank or a single specific element.

text: In requirements files, set a dependency's lower bound to the minimum STABLE release that supports the APIs and imports used by the codebase, using an inclusive lower bound and an exclusive upper bound (e.g. `{package}>=X.Y,<upper`). Avoid release candidates and avoid `>` for the lower bound, since `>X.Y,<=X.(Y+1)` excludes patch releases of the lower bound while admitting patches of the next minor — the opposite of the intent.
reason: Prevents installing a version that does not support the current import patterns (causing ImportErrors at runtime/CI) and avoids resolving to pre-release versions, keeping the constraint aligned with what the source actually requires.
common_pattern: Managing dependency version constraints in requirements/base.txt: (a) the lower bound must be the minimum stable release that supports the APIs/imports actually used, expressed with correct inclusive/exclusive semantics (`{package}>=X.Y,<upper`), and (b) when newer code needs an API that only exists in a newer release, the correct fix is to bump the pinned version constraint rather than add a compatibility import shim.

text: When code depends on a symbol/API that only exists in a newer release of a dependency, bump the pinned version constraint in requirements/base.txt instead of adding a `try/except ImportError` compatibility import; if the supported version cannot be bumped yet, keep the existing stable API rather than introducing a version-dependent shim.
reason: A try/except import workaround obscures the real version dependency, silently changes behavior based on the installed version, and is harder to maintain than either pinning the correct version or deferring the migration. The full dependency constraint set must stay in sync with the imports in the source.
common_pattern: Managing dependency version constraints in requirements/base.txt: (a) the lower bound must be the minimum stable release that supports the APIs/imports actually used, expressed with correct inclusive/exclusive semantics (`{package}>=X.Y,<upper`), and (b) when newer code needs an API that only exists in a newer release, the correct fix is to bump the pinned version constraint rather than add a compatibility import shim.

text: Generate migrations using the project's pinned/stable dependency versions, not dev, master, or pre-release builds; verify that each migration's `dependencies` entries reference migration names that exist in those versions before committing.
reason: Migrations created against a dependency's master/dev branch or a pre-release framework can contain bogus dependency references or unstable output that fails on the versions the project actually ships.
common_pattern: Migrations must be generated against stable, pinned/targeted dependency versions—not dev, master, or pre-release builds—and their dependency references must be verified before committing.

text: Use `additional_dependencies` in a pre-commit hook only for extra plugins or dependencies that the hook environment does not already provide or pin via its `rev`; do not add them solely to duplicate pins or keep versions synchronized with `package.json`.
reason: Generalization 5 describes a distinct sub-pattern within pre-commit configuration: dependency pinning semantics for `additional_dependencies`.
common_pattern: Pre-commit configuration should be scoped to the project's actual file types, tooling, and dependencies rather than copied wholesale from another project's setup.

text: Remove temporary workarounds and obsolete configuration (e.g., CLI flags in build scripts) once the upstream dependency change that made them unnecessary is available in the project's version; when adding such workarounds, reference the upstream issue/PR that will obsolete them.
reason: Prevents carrying dead compatibility code and outdated build invocations, reducing maintenance burden and avoiding conflicts with upstream behavior.
common_pattern: Removing obsolete code or configuration once an upstream dependency change makes them unnecessary

text: In Dockerfiles, choose the smallest base image that satisfies the project's requirements (e.g., `python:<version>-slim`). Pin the base image to the project's target Python version and keep it in sync with the version declared in packaging and CI configuration (e.g., `python:3.12-slim`). If a heavier base image is needed (e.g., full debian-based `python:<version>` for preinstalled system packages or compiler stability), document the reason and the expected size impact. Reference/example Dockerfiles intended as best-practice templates should favor simplicity and avoid unnecessary layers or tooling.
reason: Smaller images improve pull/deploy times and reduce storage cost, while pinning the base image to the project's target Python version avoids drift from the runtime the project is developed and tested against. Beginner-facing reference examples should not propagate unnecessary bloat.
scope: Dockerfile base image selection / container build configuration, especially beginner-facing project templates
common_pattern: Dockerfile base-image selection best practices: prefer minimal/slim base images, justify heavier images, and keep the base image version in sync with the project's target runtime.

text:
In HTML templates, keep markup semantic: place user-facing text inside its enclosing semantic element (e.g., paragraph text inside `

`), and implement decorative prefixes, separators, or line breaks via CSS pseudo-elements rather than hardcoded HTML entities or `
` elements.
reason: Separates content from presentation and ensures templates render and style correctly with valid, semantic markup.
common_pattern: Semantic HTML template authoring: keep user-facing content in appropriate semantic elements and delegate purely presentational embellishments to CSS rather than hardcoding them in markup.

text: When a refactor makes existing CSS selectors or class hooks unused, remove them from both the templates/markup and the corresponding stylesheet rules in the same change rather than leaving dead or redundant CSS behind.
reason: Prevents dead rules from accumulating, keeps CSS maintainable, and avoids confusing future maintainers about which styles are actually in use.
common_pattern: Dead CSS cleanup during refactors: when markup or refactoring changes make CSS selectors/classes unused, remove them in the same change rather than leaving orphaned rules or conflicting styles.

text: In CSS, define font sizes with relative units (`rem`/`em`/`%`) instead of `px`, and define `line-height` as a unitless proportional value (e.g., `line-height: 1.5;`) so text scales with the element's font-size and respects user browser font-size preferences.
reason: Relative font sizes and unitless line-heights scale automatically with user font-size settings and browser zoom, improving accessibility and responsiveness; fixed `px` values override user preferences and break text resizing.
common_pattern: CSS values should use unitless or relative units rather than absolute `px`, either to enable scaling with user/browser font settings (font-size, line-height) or as a convention where units are redundant (zero values).

text: Omit units for zero CSS values (write `0`, not `0px`).
reason: Shorter and conventional CSS; the unit is redundant for zero and its presence is unnecessary.
common_pattern: CSS values should use unitless or relative units rather than absolute `px`, either to enable scaling with user/browser font settings (font-size, line-height) or as a convention where units are redundant (zero values).

text: Avoid `!important` for routine responsive and state overrides. Instead, resolve specificity conflicts naturally: write base selectors as class-only (e.g., `.nav-pills > .breads` instead of `.nav-pills > li.breads`) and make override selectors target the same class being overridden (e.g., `.nav-pills > .presentation`) so specificity matches and source order decides the winner.
reason: `!important` breaks the natural cascade and makes later intentional overrides harder. Element-qualified selectors unnecessarily raise specificity, forcing `!important` in media queries or state overrides. Keeping specificity low and predictable lets source order and normal cascade rules apply overrides cleanly.
common_pattern: Avoid `!important` in CSS by keeping selector specificity low and matching it between base and override rules

text: Apply hover styles and pointer cursors only to actual interactive elements (e.g., `a` tags, buttons), not to non-clickable container elements. If a container should visually react on hover, either scope the CSS to the interactive child or make the container itself the interactive element. Avoid decorative hover effects on non-interactive content imagery unless they clearly improve the UI.
reason: Misleading hover affordances on non-clickable areas confuse users about click targets; decorative hover effects add complexity for marginal benefit.
common_pattern: Visual affordances (hover styles, pointer cursors, link underlines) must accurately reflect interactivity and remain accessible.

text: Preserve link underlines (or another clear visual affordance beyond color alone) on inline links in body content. Do not remove link underlines globally with `text-decoration: none`; if underlines are removed for non-content UI links, scope the removal or restore underlines for links within text, including hover states.
reason: Links relying only on color are hard to distinguish from surrounding text, reducing usability and accessibility.
common_pattern: Visual affordances (hover styles, pointer cursors, link underlines) must accurately reflect interactivity and remain accessible.

text: In bakerydemo/static/css/main.css, follow the project CSS conventions: do not duplicate styles already provided by Bootstrap (check the framework source first), keep the Utilities section last so it can override component styles, and use project-defined CSS custom properties consistently with correct var(...) fallbacks.
reason: These practices keep the custom stylesheet minimal, predictable under the CSS cascade, and consistent with the project's design tokens, reducing maintenance burden and visual bugs.
common_pattern: CSS maintainability conventions for bakerydemo/static/css/main.css: avoid duplicating framework-provided styles, preserve project section ordering so utilities can override components, and use project-defined CSS custom properties consistently with correct fallbacks.

text: For adjacent min-width/max-width media queries, do not let the ranges overlap: because both are inclusive, offset the boundary by 1px (e.g., max-width: 991px with min-width: 992px). Do not set min-width and max-width to the same value; use width instead when a fixed size is intended.
reason: Inclusive media query boundaries can cause multiple blocks to apply at the same exact width, producing conflicting or redundant styles.
common_pattern: Responsive breakpoint handling: use consistent, named breakpoint values and scope media-query overrides correctly to avoid gaps, overlaps, and unintended global responsive behavior.

text: Compose management commands by invoking existing commands via call_command() instead of duplicating their logic or side effects; verify subcommand behavior before adding explicit steps.
reason: Reuses the canonical implementation, avoids divergent behavior, redundant work, and sequencing errors, and keeps management commands composable.
common_pattern: Composing Django management commands by reusing existing commands via call_command() instead of duplicating logic or side effects

text: In gallery/image-card templates, do not use heading elements (h1–h6) for individual image titles or captions; rely on the image's alt text for its accessible name, and only render a visible non-heading title/caption when it adds context beyond the alt text.
reason: Headings define document section hierarchy and are semantically misleading for standalone images. Repeating alt text as visible title/caption creates redundant content and noise for users and assistive technology.
common_pattern: In gallery/image-card templates, image titles should not be marked up as headings, and visible titles/captions should not merely duplicate the image's alt text.

text: In Django/Wagtail templates, render rich text model fields with the `|richtext` filter, not `|safe`. Avoid `|safe` unless unescaped output is explicitly required — it disables Django's autoescaping, bypasses Wagtail's rich-text feature handling, and causes rendering glitches.
reason: `|safe` disables HTML escaping (XSS risk on editable content) and skips Wagtail's dedicated rich-text processing, producing unintended markup glitches.
common_pattern: Template-layer rendering of model fields: three generalizations converge on using the correct Wagtail/Django template filter (`|richtext`) rather than `|safe`, and a fourth shifts the same theme to avoiding presentation-layer manipulation (template truncation) of curated model fields.

text: For @font-face declarations, use the same font file format as existing fonts in the project (e.g., .woff) rather than introducing new formats like .ttf, .otf, or .woff2.
reason: Both generalizations address font format selection for @font-face; the first suggests using a single modern format (woff2 only), while the second resolves to matching the existing project convention (.woff). The consistent principle is to avoid mixing formats and adhere to the established project convention.
common_pattern: Consistent font file format in @font-face declarations across the project

text: Scope demo/environment notices to the specific admin/login screens where they belong, and implement them by reusing existing UI components (e.g., `help_block`) rather than injecting a global banner into every HTML response via middleware.
reason: Global notices distract from many page designs and are harder to maintain; scoping them and reusing existing components keeps auxiliary messaging unobtrusive and consistent with the product's visual design.
common_pattern: Auxiliary/demo-environment notices should not be injected globally into every HTML response; they should be scoped to the relevant screens and reuse the project's existing UI components instead of introducing custom global banner UI.

text: End every source file, including templates, with exactly one trailing newline — do not omit the final newline and do not leave extra trailing blank lines.
reason: A single terminating newline matches standard text-file conventions and avoids 'No newline at end of file' diff noise, while removing extra blank lines prevents meaningless whitespace-only changes in version control.
common_pattern: File-ending whitespace hygiene: every text file (including HTML templates) must terminate with exactly one trailing newline — no missing final newline and no extra blank lines.

text: In templates, conditionally render optional metadata fields—including their surrounding separators, labels, and container tags—only when the backing value exists, instead of emitting empty elements or dangling punctuation.
reason: Suppressing optional metadata and its formatting context when unset keeps rendered output clean and avoids misleading or awkward markup such as empty meta tags, blank captions, or stray separators.
common_pattern: Optional template metadata should be conditionally rendered along with any associated separators or labels, so absent values do not produce empty tags or dangling punctuation.

text:
For block `preview_value` sample/demo content in `blocks.py`, use content that faithfully matches the block's real format and provenance: rich-text previews must use valid rich-text markup (e.g. wrap paragraph content in `

...

`), and embedded media must be project-owned or have verified licensing/provenance (e.g. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0) rather than arbitrary third-party URLs. `data-block-key` is not required in preview values.
reason: Technically accurate, project-owned preview content keeps demo data consistent with the block's actual format and ensures media stays available with known licensing.
scope: global for `preview_value` definitions involving rich-text or media child blocks
common_pattern: All three generalizations concern the quality and correctness of block preview/demo content (preview_value definitions in blocks.py and static preview assets in templates/base/preview/*.html): the demo content should faithfully represent the real block format, carry verified provenance, and be lightweight/theme-friendly.

text: Use SVG assets for static block preview images in preview templates (e.g. `templates/base/preview/*.html`) instead of raster PNGs, to keep the preview lightweight and easy to restyle for themes/dark mode.
reason: SVGs reduce payload size and are easier to re-theme (including dark mode) than raster images.
common_pattern: All three generalizations concern the quality and correctness of block preview/demo content (preview_value definitions in blocks.py and static preview assets in templates/base/preview/*.html): the demo content should faithfully represent the real block format, carry verified provenance, and be lightweight/theme-friendly.

text: Use 4-space indentation in CSS files to keep formatting consistent with the project's Python indentation style and avoid mixing 2-space and 4-space indentation.
reason: Mixed indentation widths are visually inconsistent; matching the project's Python convention (4 spaces) keeps CSS formatting simple and uniform across languages.
common_pattern: Both generalizations state the same convention: use 4-space indentation in CSS files to stay consistent with the project's Python indentation style and avoid mixed 2/4-space indentation. The second generalization is a bare '+1' agreement with the first, confirming convergence rather than introducing a new pattern.

text: In Wagtail page templates, access page fields consistently through the `page` context variable (e.g., `page.image`, `page.origin`) rather than mixing `self.field` and `page.field`.
reason: Mixing `self` and `page` in the same template is confusing; consistent `page.` access makes it clear all fields come from the same page context and matches Wagtail template conventions.
common_pattern: Both generalizations encode the same convention: within a template, access page fields through a single consistent context variable (`page.field`) rather than mixing `self.field` and `page.field`.

text: In StreamField and custom block definitions, use Wagtail's built-in blocks (e.g. `ImageBlock`) directly when no extra fields are needed; pass a single block straight to `StreamField` rather than wrapping it in a single-block `StreamBlock`. Reserve custom wrapper blocks only for behavior they actually add, and name them after that behavior (e.g. `CaptionedImageBlock`) rather than shadowing the built-in block they relate to. When a custom block adds a field such as `caption`, compose its image field with `ImageChooserBlock` instead of nesting Wagtail's `ImageBlock`, to avoid overlapping alt-text fields.
reason: Avoids unnecessary abstraction, prevents confusion with built-in blocks, and avoids duplicate or ambiguous fields in the editor UI.
scope: Wagtail StreamField and custom block definitions
common_pattern: Wagtail StreamField/block composition conventions in bakerydemo: prefer using Wagtail's built-in blocks directly and keep custom wrapper blocks minimal, purpose-named, and only for genuinely added behavior.

text: Use the project's standard breakpoint values consistently across media queries; do not introduce near-duplicate one-off values (e.g., use 768px rather than 766px). Where shared, define breakpoints centrally as named CSS custom properties (e.g., --breakpoint-md in :root) and reference those names in media queries. Declare styles that apply at every viewport size in the selector's base rule, and reserve media queries for breakpoint-specific overrides. Scope responsive image dimension overrides such as width: auto or height: auto to the specific breakpoint that needs them rather than applying them globally.
reason: Consistent, centralized breakpoints prevent responsive-layout fragmentation, and keeping viewport-independent styles in base rules prevents styles from being unintentionally scoped to or excluded from breakpoints. Scoping responsive image dimension overrides avoids oversized or distorted images at intermediate viewport sizes.
common_pattern: Responsive breakpoint handling: use consistent, named breakpoint values and scope media-query overrides correctly to avoid gaps, overlaps, and unintended global responsive behavior.

text: Always declare colors and font-family stacks via project CSS custom properties (`var(--name)` defined in `:root`) rather than hardcoding values; this includes named color literals like `white` and hex/rgb/rgba values. When a variable includes a generic fallback, ensure it matches the font's actual classification (e.g. `serif` for Marcellus).
reason: Centralizing the palette and typography through variables keeps a single source of truth, prevents mixed variable/literal styling, and makes global theme changes less error-prone; fallback font classifications must also stay accurate.
common_pattern: CSS custom properties (design tokens) should be used consistently in stylesheets: variables must be referenced instead of hardcoded values for colors and fonts, and variables must be named by broad semantic role that reflects actual usage rather than by ordinal rank or a single specific element.

text: In templates, use native semantic HTML elements instead of generic elements with explicit ARIA landmark roles (e.g. `<footer>` instead of `<div role="contentinfo">`, `<nav>` instead of `<div role="navigation">`). Do not add explicit ARIA landmark roles to native elements that already imply them; reserve role attributes for generic elements that have no semantic equivalent.
reason: Native elements expose implicit landmark roles to assistive technologies, so explicit roles are redundant, add noise, and can conflict with native semantics.
common_pattern: Correct, non-redundant use of ARIA in HTML/Django templates: prefer native semantic elements and their implicit roles over explicit ARIA roles, and apply ARIA attributes only where the spec supports them and with semantics that don't duplicate what's already exposed.

text: Only apply ARIA attributes on elements whose role the ARIA spec supports (e.g. `aria-level` only on headings, not links or list items). Ensure `aria-label` values describe a landmark's distinct purpose rather than repeating the implicit landmark role name (e.g. "Main", not "Primary site navigation").
reason: ARIA attributes are role-specific; using them on unsupported elements has no effect for assistive tech and misleads maintainers, while labels repeating the announced role produce redundant, verbose screen-reader output.
common_pattern: Correct, non-redundant use of ARIA in HTML/Django templates: prefer native semantic elements and their implicit roles over explicit ARIA roles, and apply ARIA attributes only where the spec supports them and with semantics that don't duplicate what's already exposed.

text: Do not use `[role=...]` attribute selectors as CSS hooks; style with class selectors instead, since ARIA roles are semantic accessibility attributes and may be absent or invalid in the markup.
reason: Coupling CSS to role attributes creates dead styles tied to roles that may not exist, and misuses accessibility semantics for presentation.
common_pattern: Correct, non-redundant use of ARIA in HTML/Django templates: prefer native semantic elements and their implicit roles over explicit ARIA roles, and apply ARIA attributes only where the spec supports them and with semantics that don't duplicate what's already exposed.

text: When building reusable templates or component partials, extract shared markup into common includes or base templates and override only the differing blocks. Keep reused pieces free of page-, site-, environment-, or context-specific markup (e.g., demo/noindex directives, fixed semantic wrappers like <li>); let the child template or calling template provide the appropriate metadata or wrapper.
reason: Duplicated templates drift out of sync, and hardcoded site-specific or wrapper details make shared includes less reusable, more error-prone, and likely to propagate unintended behavior when copied.
common_pattern: Reusable templates and component partials should be factored into shared includes/base templates and kept context-agnostic, with page-, site-, or caller-specific markup provided by the child or calling template.

text: Do not truncate curated summary model fields (e.g. `introduction`) in templates. If the design needs a shorter value, set the length limit on the model field definition instead.
reason: Template truncation defeats the purpose of a curated field and obscures its intended length; a model-level constraint keeps content valid and lets the design work without presentation-layer truncation.
common_pattern: Template-layer rendering of model fields: three generalizations converge on using the correct Wagtail/Django template filter (`|richtext`) rather than `|safe`, and a fourth shifts the same theme to avoiding presentation-layer manipulation (template truncation) of curated model fields.

text: For interactive controls, ensure one clear accessible name and do not override existing visible labels: use an action-oriented `aria-label` for icon-only or ambiguous controls, avoid adding a `<label>` when the control already has `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby`, and keep visible text labels stable while exposing state changes through ARIA attributes such as `aria-pressed`.
reason: Multiple reviewers converged on ARIA/accessibility labeling best practices: screen reader users need action-oriented names, duplicate labeling mechanisms create redundancy/confusion, and replacing visible labels can unintentionally change UI text users rely on.
common_pattern: Accessible naming and state handling for interactive controls: use ARIA attributes intentionally, avoid redundant or conflicting labeling mechanisms, and preserve visible labels.

text: In Wagtail projects, do not model repeated or featured content sections as hard-coded numbered scalar fields (e.g. `featured_section_1..N`) or hard-code near-identical markup blocks in templates. Instead, use a reusable abstraction: for sections that should show current content, add a model method/property that queries the items dynamically; for editor-managed ordered sections, define an `Orderable` child model with a `ForeignKey` to `wagtailcore.Page` and manage it via an inline panel; in templates, iterate the resulting queryset (or repeatable model field/InlinePanel) in a single loop. When a listing should be capped, use Django's `slice` filter (e.g. `slice:"6"`), which also renders correctly when fewer items are available. Do not use `slice`/limit on relations (e.g. author lists) whose full contents are meant to be shown — present the complete data and handle layout/clutter in CSS.
reason: Merges the DRY loop requirement, the Wagtail-specific model abstractions (dynamic query methods and Orderable child models with inline panels), and the two complementary `slice` conditions: `slice` is appropriate for intentionally capping variable-length child listings, but must not be used to truncate relations that are meant to display all fetched items.
common_pattern: Data-driven Django/Wagtail template rendering: let the template iterate over querysets rather than hard-coding repeated markup or truncating data inconsistently, and use `slice` only where it intentionally caps variable-length listings.

text: For model/page docstrings and inline comments, use precise, accurate terminology that describes the actual ORM/storage behavior, concrete fields, capabilities, and constraints; avoid vague or misleading wording such as 'independently of the database', 'preview', or 'any type of page content'. When documenting allowed child-page constraints, prefer 'Specifies that ...' over 'Defines that ...'.
reason: Precise documentation prevents maintainers and developers from misreading what a model/page class actually does, what fields it supports, and how it interacts with the database. This also keeps comment style consistent for constraints.
common_pattern: Model/page documentation and inline comments must use precise, accurate terminology that reflects actual ORM/storage behavior, capabilities, fields, and constraints, rather than vague or misleading wording.

text: Comments and docstrings that mention another code entity by name — such as a signal, function, environment variable, or configuration key — must use the exact current name as defined or read in the code, and must be kept accurate when that name changes.
reason: Incorrect or stale references mislead readers and operators: they may look in the wrong place for related behavior or set an environment variable that the code never reads.
common_pattern: Comments and docstrings must reference code entities by their exact current names so readers are not misled by stale, variant, or mismatched references.

text: In README setup documentation, scope each section to a concrete supported environment or tool, and document only the primary supported setup method; fold conditional steps for subsets of users into the relevant setup section, and avoid duplicating basic upstream installation steps when linking to an upstream guide.
reason: Keeps setup instructions clear, accurate, and maintainable by preventing misleading sections and redundant instructions that can diverge from upstream docs.
common_pattern: README setup documentation should be audience-scoped, non-duplicative, and consistently structured, especially around setup methods, conditional steps, and dependency lists.

text: When README setup sections list prerequisites, use a consistent `### Dependencies` heading with bulleted, linked entries across every setup method, and mark optional tools as `(Optional)`; list tools such as Virtualenv/VirtualenvWrapper as dependencies rather than only mentioning them in prose.
reason: Makes dependencies scannable and comparable across setup methods and follows existing documentation conventions.
common_pattern: README setup documentation should be audience-scoped, non-duplicative, and consistently structured, especially around setup methods, conditional steps, and dependency lists.

text: In bakerydemo setup documentation and settings docs, only document settings modules that are valid entrypoints selectable via DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE; do not document auto-loaded modules as standalone entrypoints or reference obsolete settings modules. Keep README instructions consistent with the current settings/env configuration: specify a valid DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE (e.g., bakerydemo.settings.dev) for .env so the project is immediately runnable, and do not describe optional files such as .env or bakerydemo/settings/local.py as strictly required for the server to start.
reason: Prevents documentation from referencing invalid or obsolete settings modules, avoids documenting auto-loaded modules as standalone entrypoints, and keeps local setup instructions accurate so users are not left with an empty or misconfigured .env or the false impression that optional configuration files are required.
common_pattern: Bakerydemo setup documentation must remain accurate, complete, and consistent with the current Django settings/env configuration so users can run the project immediately without misleading or obsolete instructions.

text: In user-facing documentation, labels, and help text, use terminology and example content that are familiar and appropriate for the target audience and project domain — avoid technical implementation jargon and unrelated pop-culture references. In the bakery demo, placeholder/sample content such as StreamField preview values, fixtures, and seed data should be bread- or bakery-themed rather than generic Lorem ipsum or unrelated filler, because demo content also serves as documentation and should reinforce the demo's theme.
reason: Audience-appropriate, domain-aligned wording and examples improve user comprehension and avoid confusing or out-of-place references; in the bakery demo, theme-consistent sample content makes the showcase coherent and illustrative.
common_pattern: User-facing text should use terminology and examples that are familiar, audience-appropriate, and consistent with the project's domain or locale, rather than technical jargon or unrelated references.

text: For fixture-export documentation, rely on the export command's own exclusion flags (e.g., dumpdata's -e) as the single source of truth; do not also document manual SQL delete/cleanup steps for the same tables.
reason: The export command defines what is excluded. Duplicating that logic with manual SQL makes the docs redundant and prone to drift.
common_pattern: Fixture/data-file hygiene: fixture files should contain only intentional seed/demo data, and documentation about fixture preparation should not duplicate the fixture tooling's own exclusion logic. The cluster splits into two related-but-distinct sub-patterns: (a) what belongs in fixture content, and (b) how fixture preparation is documented.

text: When adding or updating documentation links, use stable, version-agnostic URLs (e.g., `latest`, `stable`) or authoritative sources (e.g., repository tags/releases page, project-scoped pages) instead of version-pinned, deprecated, or manually maintained links; verify that links work.
reason: Version-pinned, deprecated, or manually duplicated links become stale or broken as upstream projects change, making documentation unreliable.
common_pattern: Documentation links should reference stable, version-agnostic, or authoritative sources rather than version-pinned, deprecated, or manually duplicated ones to avoid stale or broken links.

text: Keep demo-project deployment artifacts in sync: if a platform-specific deployment config exists (e.g., `app.json`, `heroku.yml`, Dockerfile references), keep matching deployment instructions in the README; if a platform config file is removed, remove or replace all references to that platform in the docs. Conversely, do not document or recommend a deployment host that has no corresponding config/support in the repo.
reason: Stale or mismatched deployment docs either direct users to unsupported methods or hide a supported low-friction deployment path, causing confusion and failed setups.
scope: demo project deployment documentation and configuration
common_pattern: Deployment documentation and deployment configuration/manifests in demo projects must stay consistent with each other — neither endorsing a host without a corresponding config/quick-deploy path, nor leaving docs referencing platforms whose config files have been removed.

text: Write docstrings and comments in complete, grammatically correct English and make them sufficiently self-explanatory: avoid redundant preposition combinations, omitted subjects, missing articles, and incorrect verb forms; include reasons for evaluative claims; and describe module/class purpose at the full breadth of supported use cases.
reason: Clear, correct, and complete documentation improves readability, professionalism, and understanding of design tradeoffs and supported behavior.
common_pattern: Docstrings and comments should be high-quality developer-facing documentation: grammatically correct, complete, and sufficiently explanatory.

text: When documentation depends on cache-based prebuilds or other cached build artifacts, add a scheduled CI job to refresh the cache and document how users can detect or verify that they are not receiving stale artifacts.
reason: Cache-based prebuilds can silently go stale, so documented workflows may serve outdated builds; a scheduled refresh keeps the cache fresh, while detection/verification instructions let users know when the cache is stale.
common_pattern: Documentation that depends on cached/prebuilt artifacts must define the artifact freshness lifecycle: both a scheduled mechanism to refresh stale caches and user-facing guidance to detect or verify staleness.

text: For live demo site banner copy, use a generic or approximate reset cadence (e.g., "daily", "periodically") rather than hardcoding specific reset times or linking to external time zones; the reset schedule is deployment-specific and not defined in the repository.
reason: Avoids coupling the reusable demo-banner feature to a specific schedule or external domain, reducing maintenance when reset settings change.
common_pattern: Both generalizations address the same concern: demo-site banner copy should avoid hardcoding deployment-specific reset times, using generic/approximate cadence instead.

text: Write comments in configuration and example/template files as reader-oriented documentation: explain the file's or setting's purpose and intent, and give actionable instructions where relevant, rather than describing team conventions with 'we/our' language or only listing contents.
reason: Instructive, purpose-oriented comments help new contributors and users understand why the file or setting exists and how to use it.
scope: configuration files, example/template files, and related code comments
common_pattern: Documentation comments in configuration and example/template files should be reader-oriented: they should explain purpose/intent and tell the reader what to do, rather than describe the team's conventions or merely list file contents.

text: In documentation, describe framework or dependency support as "compatible"/"compatibility" rather than "compliant"/"compliance", reserving compliance language for formal adherence to a specification or regulation.
reason: "Compatible" accurately describes interoperability; "compliant" implies conformance to a standard, which is a different and potentially misleading claim.
common_pattern: Distinguishing between testing/compatibility intent versus formal compliance/production configuration when documenting security-related features (e.g., CSP).

text: When a configuration or code file exists to test a framework's compatibility (e.g., CSP directives validating a web framework), state that testing intent explicitly in the file's description so it isn't mistaken for recommended production configuration.
reason: Clarifies that the settings are for validation/testing purposes and prevents readers from adopting them as production recommendations.
common_pattern: Distinguishing between testing/compatibility intent versus formal compliance/production configuration when documenting security-related features (e.g., CSP).

text: In Markdown fenced code blocks (```...```), write code verbatim: do not wrap content in inline-code backticks and do not indent the code unnecessarily. Inline backticks belong in prose for code fragments, and indentation is only needed for indented code blocks or for nesting code blocks under list items.
reason: Fenced code blocks preserve content literally, so extra backticks or indentation render as part of the code, creating visual noise or over-indented output in documentation.
common_pattern: Both generalizations address the same Markdown documentation pitfall: fenced code blocks render their contents literally, so adding inline-code backticks or unnecessary indentation inside them produces unwanted visible formatting instead of clean code output.

text: In demo/example filter sets such as BreadPageFilterSet, avoid repeating the same filter type; vary filter classes so examples demonstrate distinct filter variants, e.g. ModelChoiceFilter on an FK, ModelMultipleChoiceFilter on an FK, and ModelMultipleChoiceFilter on ParentalManyToMany.
reason: Example code should demonstrate distinct framework capabilities rather than repeat the same functionality, making the demo more useful and instructive.
common_pattern: Demo/example filter sets should showcase distinct filter variants instead of repeating the same filter type, so the example demonstrates different framework capabilities.

text: Keep shared/base configuration minimal and portable: limit `requirements/base.txt`, `settings/base.py`, and `.env.example` to dependencies and settings needed across all environments. Move environment-specific, deployment-specific, or optional/developer-convenience dependencies and settings to environment-specific files (e.g., `requirements/production.txt`, local/dev or deployment settings modules), and scope environment template files by execution context (e.g., use `.env.docker.example` for container-only variables rather than adding them to the shared `.env.example`). Ensure Dockerfile default `ENV` contains only production-safe, image-general defaults (e.g., debug disabled, production settings module) — do not bake deployment- or project-specific environment values into the image, and supply those at runtime. Expose operationally tunable values through environment variables rather than hardcoded constants.
reason: Shared configuration stays portable and minimal, avoiding leaking container-only or deployment-specific values into non-container workflows (e.g., virtualenv/local dev onboarding). Production-safe image defaults keep images secure by default, while runtime injection of deployment-specific values keeps the image decoupled from any single target and preserves deploy-time flexibility.
common_pattern: Shared/base configuration files should contain only cross-environment essentials; environment-specific, deployment-specific, optional, or developer-convenience dependencies and settings belong in environment-specific files or environment variables.

text: Fixture files should contain only records needed to initialize site/demo content. Omit transient usage/analytics/tracking data (e.g., search queries, daily hit counts), and do not silently remove data values (blanking URLs or fields) unless that removal is the explicit intent of the change.
reason: Keeps fixtures focused on reproducible setup data and prevents accidental edits from breaking demo content or masking unintended changes. Covers both sides of curation: what to add and what not to strip.
common_pattern: Fixture/data-file hygiene: fixture files should contain only intentional seed/demo data, and documentation about fixture preparation should not duplicate the fixture tooling's own exclusion logic. The cluster splits into two related-but-distinct sub-patterns: (a) what belongs in fixture content, and (b) how fixture preparation is documented.

text: Do not hardcode third-party API keys, external service links, or deployment/configuration-dependent values in templates; define them as settings variables and inject them into the template context, or omit non-essential external links.
reason: Centralizes configuration, supports per-environment values, avoids exposing credentials in source templates, and prevents templates from imposing brittle or maintenance-heavy external dependencies.
common_pattern: Avoid embedding external-service credentials, URLs, or deployment/configuration-dependent values directly in templates; centralize such values in settings/context or omit non-essential external references.

text: Do not duplicate configuration settings definitions; ensure each setting is defined only once in the canonical settings module (e.g., settings/base.py).
reason: Duplicate settings definitions are redundant and can cause confusion about which value takes effect; keeping a single definition preserves a clear source of truth.
common_pattern: Maintain clarity and a single source of truth in settings configuration, covering both code definitions and documentation of entrypoints.

text: Do not add global lint-rule suppressions (e.g., flake8 ignore codes in setup.cfg) to work around a localized code issue; fix the offending code or use a scoped suppression, and remove any global suppression once the code that required it is gone.
reason: Global suppressions hide violations project-wide and become stale; scoped fixes keep linting effective and configuration accurate.
common_pattern: Both generalizations concern global lint-rule suppressions in setup.cfg: avoid adding them to work around localized issues, and remove them when the offending code is removed.

text: Gate optional features behind a dedicated feature flag or environment-variable conditional, and keep all settings that enable or configure that feature inside the same guard rather than reusing unrelated settings or placing them outside the guard.
reason: Dedicated gating decouples feature availability from unrelated security/config concerns and ensures the feature remains inert unless explicitly enabled via its own flag or environment variable.
common_pattern: Feature-flag/configuration hygiene: optional functionality must be gated by a dedicated, clearly-scoped toggle, and all related settings should live inside that same guard rather than being coupled to unrelated flags or configured outside the guard.

text: When enforcing restrictions on protected/admin users (e.g. preventing password or username changes), apply the guard comprehensively: use Wagtail hooks such as `before_edit_user` to prevent the action rather than correcting it afterward, remove or gate alternate admin routes like `/django-admin/` in `urls.py` (Django admin actions bypass Wagtail hooks), and enforce all security-critical fields including `is_superuser` and `is_active`, not just credentials.
reason: Partial admin protections are trivially bypassed — via `/django-admin/`, which does not trigger Wagtail hooks, or by flipping other privileged flags such as `is_superuser`/`is_active`. Complete enforcement prevents lockout bypass and privilege escalation.
common_pattern: When enforcing restrictions on privileged/admin accounts, close every bypass path and cover every security-critical field — not just the most obvious one — because partial enforcement can be circumvented through alternate admin routes or by changing other privileged flags.

text: For public demo deployments, block all write operations to admin/content rather than guarding only individual fields; if a read-only admin login cannot be enforced, disable admin access entirely and direct users to Gitpod to try admin features.
reason: Any permitted write path on a public demo risks upload of malicious or abusive material; field-level restrictions leave other write paths exposed.
common_pattern: When enforcing restrictions on privileged/admin accounts, close every bypass path and cover every security-critical field — not just the most obvious one — because partial enforcement can be circumvented through alternate admin routes or by changing other privileged flags.

text: Do not place a Django `AppConfig` override for one app inside an unrelated shared/base app (e.g., `{project}/base/apps.py`). Give the override its own dedicated home — either a local app package named after the app being replaced (e.g., `{project}/images/`) or an `apps.py` at the project package root (`{project}/apps.py`) — and reference it from `INSTALLED_APPS` by module path (e.g., `"{project}.images"` or `"{project}.apps"`) rather than by a fully qualified `"path.to.apps.AppConfig"` entry, letting Django auto-discover the config.
reason: Keeps app configuration scoped to its own app boundary, avoids confusing/unrelated overrides in a base app, avoids importing unrelated app code into shared settings modules, and follows Django's automatic `AppConfig` discovery behavior.
common_pattern: A Django `AppConfig` that overrides a built-in or third-party app should not be nestled inside an unrelated shared/base app (e.g., `{project}/base/apps.py`); it belongs in its own dedicated module and should be referenced from `INSTALLED_APPS` via a simple module path so Django auto-discovers the config.

text: When adding an embed/video block that mirrors an existing video link (e.g., in `RecipeStreamBlock`), reuse the existing block's `preview_value` URL instead of introducing a different placeholder URL.
reason: Keeps media block previews consistent and avoids mismatched thumbnails or unnecessary variation between equivalent blocks.
common_pattern: Both generalizations express the same principle at different abstraction levels: a new media/embed block that duplicates an existing video link must reuse that existing block's `preview_value` URL rather than inventing a different placeholder. Generalization 2 is simply the entity-specific instance of Generalization 1.

text: Django-version-specific or database-backend-specific additions (imports, middleware, and INSTALLED_APPS entries such as django.contrib.postgres) must be guarded conditionally — a Django version check for version-gated features, and a configured-database-engine check for backend-specific apps — rather than added unconditionally.
reason: Keeps the project runnable against the minimum supported Django version and against non-Postgres databases, so new features can be merged without breaking compatibility for existing deployments.
common_pattern: Version- and backend-specific Django additions (imports, middleware, INSTALLED_APPS entries) must be conditionally guarded rather than added unconditionally, so shared configuration stays valid across all supported Django versions and database backends.

text: In `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, configure hook file filters (`files`, `types_or`) and enabled hooks to match only the languages, file extensions, and tooling actually used by the project; do not copy broader file type lists or hooks (e.g., SCSS, TypeScript, ESLint with TypeScript parser/plugins) from another project's configuration.
reason: Generalizations 1-4 all converge on limiting pre-commit configuration to the project's real file types and tooling, and avoiding copy-paste from upstream projects.
common_pattern: Pre-commit configuration should be scoped to the project's actual file types, tooling, and dependencies rather than copied wholesale from another project's setup.

text: Only declare ordering when a concrete requirement exists. Do not add unnecessary `Meta.ordering` to Django models; in Wagtail `SnippetViewSet.ordering`, specify only the fields required for the intended default sort (no extra fallback fields). For CMS-managed models, manual sort ordering should be optional/configurable rather than hard-coded into the default ordering.
reason: Unnecessary ordering introduces implicit query behavior and noise, obscures intended manual ordering, and forces a UX/policy choice on all CMS usages; keeping ordering conditional preserves flexibility and makes example/demo code demonstrate good patterns.
common_pattern: Avoid unnecessary/hard-coded ordering declarations in Django model Meta and Wagtail SnippetViewSet ordering; only specify ordering when a concrete requirement exists, and prefer making manual sort ordering optional/configurable for CMS-managed models.

text: When defining `search_fields` on Wagtail Page models (e.g., `PersonPage`), include user-searchable content fields such as `introduction` in addition to `body`, and for related fields like `origin`/`Country`, use Wagtail's `index.RelatedFields` to index the related model's searchable fields (e.g., country name) instead of only the relation ID.
reason: Search should cover the fields users expect to search against, including page content beyond the primary rich-text body and related taxonomy/location names, not just foreign-key IDs.
scope: Wagtail Page model search configuration, especially search_fields
common_pattern: Wagtail Page `search_fields` should index all user-searchable content, including non-body page fields and related-model fields, rather than indexing only `body` or relation IDs.

text: Place ENV instructions as late as possible in a Dockerfile, after expensive RUN/COPY layers, so changing environment values does not invalidate cached build steps.
reason: Docker invalidates all layers subsequent to a changed instruction, so deferring ENV preserves expensive cached build layers.
common_pattern: Docker/environment configuration hygiene: what values belong in image defaults versus runtime, how environment variables are scoped across execution contexts, and how ENV placement affects build caching.

text: In demo/sample settings files and demo/reset management commands (e.g., `reset_demo.py`), do not leave the default `changeme` admin password (or any other value that looks intentional). Use an obvious, self-descriptive placeholder/demo-safe value that signals it is not a real secret and must be changed (e.g., `demo`), or create a dedicated superuser. Keep any seed/fixture data that depends on this password in sync.
reason: A default like `changeme` can appear already-set or intentional, discouraging users from changing it and creating a shared-credential security risk; reset/seed flows should also avoid retaining it to prevent accidental demo-environment lockout for all users.
common_pattern: Demo/sample environments must not ship a shared, hardcoded default admin password like `changeme`; instead use a self-descriptive placeholder in settings and have seed/reset commands set a non-default password or create a dedicated superuser.

text: In Dockerfiles, avoid redundant Python environment indirection: rely on the container for isolation and do not add a virtualenv unless needed. If a virtualenv is used, invoke its executables via the configured PATH (e.g., `uwsgi`) and install packages with the matching interpreter (`pythonX.Y -m pip`) instead of absolute paths or bare `pip`.
reason: A virtualenv is usually redundant inside a container, but when one is configured, commands should respect the environment setup rather than bypassing PATH or installing with the wrong interpreter.
common_pattern: Dockerfile Python environment and path hygiene: avoid redundant environment indirection and rely on the container boundary or configured PATH/interpreter instead of hardcoded paths or implicit tool invocations.

text: New-developer setup must be complete and non-blocking: setup instructions should either produce a working configuration by populating required environment variables such as `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` rather than creating an empty `.env`, or the code should provide sane defaults for those variables (e.g. `manage.py` defaulting `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` to the dev settings module) and suppress/document harmless missing-`.env` warnings. In setup documentation, distinguish hard requirements for server startup from optional/recommended files (e.g. `.env` may only cause a `django-dotenv` warning, and `bakerydemo/settings/local.py` may be loaded inside a `try`/`except` so the server can still start without them). Still document optional setup files because they improve local development and prevent developers from discovering the need later.
reason: Merged because both rules are complementary framings of the same non-blocking new-developer setup requirement: one addresses code/config defaults and populated setup instructions, while the other addresses accurate setup documentation that separates hard requirements from optional/recommended files.
common_pattern: Setup documentation should accurately classify files as mandatory vs optional/recommended, while still documenting optional files that improve local development.

text: For responsive {% picture %} sizes attributes, account for device pixel density when choosing breakpoint values (e.g., use roughly half the intended CSS width for mobile) so the browser selects the smaller image source instead of jumping to the next larger variant.
reason: Browsers factor device pixel ratio into source selection; over-stating the mobile size causes the larger image variant to be downloaded, defeating responsive image sizing.
common_pattern: Responsive breakpoint handling: use consistent, named breakpoint values and scope media-query overrides correctly to avoid gaps, overlaps, and unintended global responsive behavior.
